items.question: What happens to reliability when many groups compete on a fashionable topic?
items.statement: The hotter a scientific field with more scientific teams involved, the less likely the research findings are to be true.

citations.quote: Corollary 6: The hotter a scientifi c fi eld (with more scientifi c teams involved), the less likely the research fi ndings are to be true.

items.question: Did having US federal grants make authors more likely to post their complete raw data?
items.statement: Among papers covered by a data availability policy, having US government funding did not significantly affect the proportion of papers depositing full primary data online.

citations.quote: Among papers covered by some data availability policy (n = 351), the proportion depositing full primary data online was not different when US government funding (e.g. National Institutes of Health or National Science Foundation) was listed (15% versus 12% when US funding was not listed, P = 0.42)

items.question: Did studies in living animals reproduce as well as studies without animals?
items.statement: Animal experiments were less likely to replicate than non-animal experiments.

citations.quote: Animal experiments were less likely to replicate than non-animal experiments and this may be a consequence of animal experiments eliciting smaller effect sizes on average than non-animal experiments (see main text for further discussion).

items.question: Is it realistic to run very large studies for every question scientists ask?
items.statement: Large-scale evidence is impossible to obtain for all of the millions and trillions of research questions posed in current research.

citations.quote: Moreover, large-scale evidence is impossible to obtain for all of the millions and trillions of research questions posed in current research.

items.question: Where online were most of the shared gene expression datasets hosted?
items.statement: Most of the shared gene expression datasets were located on lab websites.

citations.quote: Most data sets were located on lab websites (28), with a few found on publisher websites (4), or within public databases (6 in the Stanford Microarray Database (SMD) [8], 6 in Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) [9], 2 in ArrayExpress [10], 2 in the NCI GeneExpression Data Portal (GEDP)(gedp.nci.nih.gov); some datasets in more than one location).

items.question: What happens to reliability when many groups compete on a fashionable topic?
items.statement: A research finding is less likely to be true when more teams are involved in a scientific field in chase of statistical significance.

citations.quote: In this framework, a research fi nding is less likely to be true when the studies conducted in a fi eld are smaller; when effect sizes are smaller; when there is a greater number and lesser preselection of tested relationships; where there is greater fl exibility in designs, defi nitions, outcomes, and analytical modes; when there is greater fi nancial and other interest and prejudice; and when more teams are involved in a scientifi c fi eld in chase of statistical signifi cance.

items.question: How many people extracted the information from the sampled articles?
items.statement: Data extraction from the 500 papers was done by a single investigator.

citations.quote: Data extraction from the 500 papers was done by a single investigator (WQ) with cross-checking in the first 50 papers by two investigators (AA and MA).

items.question: Why are results from underpowered, small studies less trustworthy?
items.statement: As the statistical power decreases, the positive predictive value (PPV) for a true research finding also decreases.

citations.quote: Small sample size means smaller power and, for all functions above, the PPV for a true research fi nding decreases as power decreases towards 1 -β = 0.05.

items.question: How much did effect sizes shrink when preclinical cancer studies were repeated?
items.statement: For original positive effects reported as numerical values, the median effect size for the replications was 0.43.

citations.quote: For original positive effects that were reported as numerical values, the median effect size for the replications was 0.43, which was 85% smaller than the median of the original effect sizes (2.96).

items.question: What was the usual way that articles broke their journal's rules on data?
items.statement: When articles failed to adhere to their journal's data availability instructions, they most commonly did so by not publicly depositing microarray data.

citations.quote: Of the remaining 351 papers that were covered by some data availability policy (with or without data deposition as a condition of publication), 208/351 papers (59%) did not fully adhere to the data availability instructions of the journals they were published in, most commonly (73%) by not publicly depositing microarray data.

items.question: How often did repeat studies succeed for results that originally showed no effect?
items.statement: Combining the data for original null effects led to a third of cases showing statistically significant effects.

citations.quote: meaning that combining the data led to a third of cases showing statistically significant effects, even though the original reported a null finding.

items.question: Does making the network bigger help accuracy on the GLUE benchmark?
items.statement: Larger models lead to a strict accuracy improvement across all four datasets on selected GLUE tasks.

citations.quote: We can see that larger models lead to a strict accuracy improvement across all four datasets, even for MRPC which only has 3,600 labeled training examples, and is substantially different from the pre-training tasks.

items.question: What share of input words gets hidden at random during the masked-word objective?
items.statement: During the masked-word objective, 15% of all WordPiece tokens in each sequence are masked at random.

citations.quote: In all of our experiments, we mask 15% of all WordPiece tokens in each sequence at random.

items.question: How does publishing raw data affect citation counts in astronomy?
items.statement: Sharing raw probe data or actual microarray images did not result in additional citations for the studied trials.

citations.quote: The few trials in this cohort which, in addition to gene expression fold-change or other preprocessed information, shared their raw probe data or actual microarray images did not receive additional citations.

citations.quote: For cases in which the original was a null effect, 10 of the 15 (67%) meta-analytic effects were likewise null (p > 0.05)
